screens.title: Debugging Applications in Production with Cloud Debugger
screens.narratorSegment: When a bug only appears in production, stopping the service or redeploying to add debug logs is often impractical. Cloud Debugger gives you a different path: you can capture application state or inject temporary logs into a running instance without taking traffic offline. In this lesson you will see how snapshot points capture variables and call stacks when a specific line executes, and how logpoints let you write ephemeral log messages that appear in Cloud Logging. We’ll also cover how to enable the debugger agent, the importance of accurate module and version labels, and permission checks for safe operation. You will walk through a Cloud Run Python example where the debugger captures an intermediate value and then a logpoint injects a debug message. Finally, you’ll learn the core safety practices: limit snapshot hits, avoid capturing sensitive data, and remove temporary points after use. By the end you will understand why Cloud Debugger reduces mean time to resolution for elusive production bugs and when to prefer a snapshot versus a logpoint.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Debugging Applications in Production with Cloud Debugger

Learn how to safely inspect state, set snapshot points, and inject temporary logs into running services across App Engine, GKE, Compute Engine, and Cloud Run. This reduces disruption and helps diagnose bugs that only appear in production.

In this lesson
Set snapshot points and logpoints, enable the debugger agent, and follow safety practices when inspecting production state.
Why it matters
You can diagnose race conditions, data-specific errors, and environment-dependent bugs without redeploying or creating downtime.
Explore Key Topics
Snapshot Points
Capture variables and the call stack when a line executes, giving a frozen view of state without pausing requests.
Logpoints
Inject temporary log messages that include expressions, then view results in Cloud Logging.
Safety & Mapping
Ensure agent installation, IAM role, and correct module/version mapping to avoid confusion and overhead.
Presentation: terminal demo with code callouts and console walkthrough
Visual concept
Live Debug Flow
Agent → Snapshot / Logpoint → Console
Agent initialized with module/version labels
Set snapshot point on line, collect variable values
Use logpoints for lightweight checks over time
No live controls — this is a narrated walkthrough.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will acquire four concrete skills that make production debugging safer and faster. First, you will be able to explain what Cloud Debugger does and why non-intrusive inspection matters. That helps you choose the right tool when stopping a service is unacceptable. Second, you will learn how to set snapshot points and logpoints, and when each is the better choice to gather runtime evidence. You will practice the mental model of snapshot equals frozen state and logpoint equals streaming observation. Third, you will integrate the debugger with common GCP environments and languages by adding the debugger agent and assigning correct module and version identifiers, ensuring the console can map running code to source. Finally, you will adopt safety and operational best practices: minimal snapshot hits, permission checks, avoiding sensitive data capture, and cleaning temporary points after use. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can self-check when you have reached practical readiness.

screens.title: What is Cloud Debugger and why non-intrusive debugging matters
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud Debugger is a production-safe inspector that captures state from a running application without stopping it. Think of it as taking a photograph of program state when a particular line executes. That photograph shows local variables, globals, and the full call stack for that instant. The key advantage is that you do not interrupt live traffic. This matters because many bugs only appear under production data patterns, specific traffic levels, or timing conditions that are hard to reproduce locally. A common misconception is that non-intrusive means zero overhead — in practice the debugger minimizes impact but capturing snapshots or evaluating complex expressions can add small overhead for the first few hits. Use snapshots sparingly and prefer logpoints for repeated checks. For example, when a balance calculation occasionally returns the wrong value only under peak load, a snapshot on the calculation line reveals the exact operand values and call sequence that led to the error without forcing a restart. Remember: snapshot equals deep, momentary inspection; logpoint equals lightweight observation over time. Which will you choose when investigating an intermittent production error?

keyIdea.title: Snapshot vs impact
keyIdea.text: Cloud Debugger lets you inspect live state with minimal disruption, but snapshots are not free — use them judiciously and prefer logpoints for ongoing observation.

content.html:
Core Concept › Definition
Cloud Debugger
A non-intrusive tool to capture application state or inject temporary logs into running services. Use it to inspect variables and call stacks without stopping production.
Quick bullets
  • Snapshot points capture variables and call stack at a line hit.
  • Logpoints inject temporary log messages with expressions.
  • Designed to avoid service downtime; still use sparingly to limit overhead.
Key Takeaway

Non-intrusive inspection is ideal for diagnosing production-only bugs, but snapshots should be limited and cleaned up after use.

Concrete example
# Pseudo: intermittent balance bug # Snapshot set on the line that finalizes balance calculation current_balance = compute_balance(user) # Snapshot captures current_balance, inputs, and call stack
Misconception check: Non-intrusive does not mean invisible. The debugger captures only the first few hits by default to reduce overhead. Overusing snapshots or complex evaluated expressions can affect performance slightly.
Analogy: photograph vs video — snapshot is a photograph of state; logpoint is like a short video clip of selected variables.
When to use: snapshot for one-off deep inspections, logpoint for continuous monitoring of a value.

screens.title: Setting a Snapshot Point
screens.narratorSegment: A snapshot point lifecycle has three clear stages: placement, capture, and inspection. First, place the snapshot at a precise line in the source where you want to freeze state. In the Console you click the line number and choose a snapshot; via tooling you may set the point programmatically. Second, when a request executes and hits that line, Cloud Debugger captures a snapshot that includes local variables, global variables, and the call stack. By default the system captures only the first few hits to keep overhead low. Third, the snapshot appears in the console where you can inspect values, step through the captured stack frames, and understand the flow that produced the bug. A common mistake is placing snapshots in hot loops or frequently-run lines; that can cause many captures and unnecessary overhead. For a concrete example, set a snapshot on the intermediate calculation in a customer billing route, trigger the route with representative input, and review captured variables to find where rounding or unexpected data entered the computation. Always remove snapshot points after you finish debugging. Setting a Snapshot Point means place a snapshot at a specific source line, trigger it with a representative request, inspect the captured state, and then remove the snapshot to avoid overhead.. In practical terms, step-by-step lifecycle from set to capture to inspection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Snapshot Lifecycle
Three steps
1. Place snapshot
Open code in Console, pick a precise line and add a snapshot point with an optional condition.
2. Capture occurs
When a request hits the line, the system captures variables and call stack. Only the first hits are usually recorded to limit impact.
3. Inspect and remove
View the snapshot in Console, examine frames and values, then delete the snapshot when finished.
Key Takeaway

Snapshots are for deep, one-off investigations: set precisely, trigger with representative traffic, inspect, and clean up.

Concrete scenario
# Example: billing route # Set snapshot on line: intermediate_value = result + 5 # Trigger: curl \ # "YOUR_CLOUD_RUN_URL/calculate/10" # Inspect: num, result, intermediate_value
Misconception: snapshots do not stream logs. They capture a single instant. If you need ongoing trace of a value choose a logpoint instead.
Avoid
  • Placing snapshots inside tight loops.
  • Capturing sensitive PII without controls.

screens.title: Logpoints — lightweight, temporary logging
screens.narratorSegment: Logpoints let you inject temporary logging statements into running code so you can observe expressions over time without redeploying. Unlike snapshots, a logpoint emits a log message to Cloud Logging whenever its line is executed, and you can include expressions like user ID or action names inside the message. Use logpoints when you need repeated observations or want to monitor a value trend across requests. For instance, if you suspect a greeting service returns incorrect personalization occasionally, a logpoint that logs the resolved greeting input lets you see many instances across traffic and spot patterns. A frequent misconception is that logpoints can inspect full local state like snapshots; they can evaluate expressions but do not provide the full call-stack capture. Also avoid logging sensitive data by accident. Logpoints are ideal for low-overhead checks and for building time-based understanding of a problem before committing to a deeper snapshot capture. Logpoints — lightweight, temporary logging means logpoints stream chosen expressions to cloud logging for repeated observation; they are lightweight but do not capture the full call stack.. In practical terms, what logpoints are, when to use them, and an example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Logpoints
Logpoints
Temporary injected logs that evaluate expressions and deliver messages to Cloud Logging without redeploying.
When to use
  • Track a value over many requests.
  • Gather occurrence frequency or patterns before using a snapshot.
  • Low-overhead checks in high-traffic services.
Key Takeaway

Use logpoints for repeated, lightweight observation, and avoid capturing sensitive fields in log messages.

Concrete example
# Set a logpoint on greeting line # Message: DEBUG: Greeting for user: {user_input} # Then curl the root URL to see injected logs in Cloud Logging
Misconception check: A logpoint is not a replacement for a snapshot when you need the call stack. It is a focused log emission, not a full state capture.
Pro-tip: include only necessary expressions to reduce log volume and privacy risk.

screens.title: Agent integration and environment support
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud Debugger requires a debugger agent or library in your application so that running instances can communicate with the Cloud Debugger service. The agent is available in language-specific forms for Java, Python, Node. js, Go, and PHP. For managed environments like App Engine and Cloud Run, you typically initialize the agent early in application startup and include module and version identifiers; for GKE and Compute Engine you install the appropriate library into the container or VM. The agent authenticates using the service account attached to the runtime, which must have the Cloud Debugger Debuggee IAM role. A common pitfall is forgetting to supply accurate module or version labels. If those values do not match the source context visible in the Console, you will be unable to set points because the Console cannot map running code lines to your repository. For example, in a Python Flask app on GKE you add the googleclouddebugger enable call at boot and pass module='my-flask-app' and version='v1.0.0' so the debugger identifies the deployed source. Always initialize the agent as early as possible so the process can register before handling traffic.

keyIdea.title: Agent + mapping
keyIdea.text: Install and initialize the language agent early; ensure the service account role and accurate module/version mapping to allow snapshots and logpoints.

content.html:
Architecture › Agent & Environments
Supported environments
  • App Engine (Standard / Flexible)
  • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
  • Compute Engine
  • Cloud Run
Key requirement: include the language agent and ensure the runtime's service account has the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role so the agent can register debuggees and send snapshots/logpoints.
Concrete code hint
# Python example snippet (initialize early) import googleclouddebugger googleclouddebugger.enable(module='my-flask-app', version='v1.0.0')
Misconception: environment managed means automatic mapping. You still must provide accurate module and version labeling or integrate with source context so the Console can match source lines.
Pro-tip
Initialize the agent in your application entrypoint before creating server listeners to ensure it registers before serving traffic.

screens.title: Python Flask example: enabling the Cloud Debugger agent
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s walk through the provided Python Flask example used for Cloud Run. At the top of main dot P Y file you import the debugger library and call the enable function with module and version parameters. These values are crucial because Cloud Debugger uses them to identify which deployed source to show in the Console. In Cloud Run, environment variables K_SERVICE and K_REVISION are commonly used for module and version respectively. The code shows a try/except around enable to avoid crashing if the agent can’t initialize in a local dev environment. Inside the Flask routes the code computes values, and there are clear spots marked where you would set a snapshot or a logpoint: the intermediate calculation line is a good candidate for a snapshot to capture numeric variables, while the response construction is ideal for a logpoint to emit a greeting message. A common misconception is that adding the enable call is sufficient without checking IAM; you must ensure the service account attached to the runtime has the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role or registration will fail. This walkthrough prepares you to add the agent, deploy, and map snapshots to code.

keyIdea.title: Initialize early
keyIdea.text: Call the debugger agent enable function at application start with accurate module and version labels; guard initialization to avoid startup failures.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › main.py initialization
Initialization pattern
import os
from flask import Flask, request
import googleclouddebugger

try:
  googleclouddebugger.enable(
    module=os.environ.get('K_SERVICE', 'my-cloud-run-service'),
    version=os.environ.get('K_REVISION', 'default')
  )
  print("Cloud Debugger enabled.")
except Exception as e:
  print(f"Failed to enable Cloud Debugger: {e}")
Note: guard the call so local testing without credentials doesn't break startup. Use environment-provided module/version values in managed runtimes.
Where to set points
Set a snapshot on intermediate calculations such as intermediate_value = result + 5 to capture num, result, and intermediate_value. Set a logpoint on response construction to emit a debug message including user_input.
Misconception: the enable call alone will not allow snapshots if the service account lacks the required IAM role. Confirm Cloud Debugger Debuggee permission for the runtime's service account.

screens.title: Using the Console and gcloud to set points
screens.narratorSegment: There are two primary interaction patterns: using the GCP Console source viewer and using the gcloud CLI. In the Console you navigate to Cloud Debugger, select your project, choose the running service, open the source file and click a line number to add a snapshot or logpoint. The Console then waits for a hit and will display captured snapshots with variables and stack frames. With the gcloud CLI you can script point creation and removal, which is useful for repeatable debugging tasks during an incident. To trigger a snapshot or logpoint, send representative traffic to the service — for example use curl to call the specific endpoint that executes your target line. After triggering, the Console shows the snapshot result; inspect variables and call frames to see the runtime context. Common errors include mismatched source mapping and insufficient IAM roles. If a snapshot never appears, check that the agent initialized, that module/version match your deployed code, and that the runtime service account has the debugger debuggee role. Always remove points when finished to avoid lingering overhead and log noise. Using the Console and gcloud to set points means place points in the console or via gcloud, trigger them with representative requests, inspect snapshots or logs, and then delete points to minimize impact.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Console & CLI
Console flow
Open Cloud Debugger in the Console, select your service, open the file, and click a line number to add a snapshot or logpoint. Wait for a hit and inspect captured state.
Trigger example
# Trigger snapshot curl "YOUR_CLOUD_RUN_URL/calculate/10" # Check the Cloud Debugger console for the captured snapshot
gcloud usage
You can script point create/remove with gcloud for repeatable debugging during incidents. Use scripted commands cautiously and remove points after use.
Troubleshooting: If points do not appear, verify the agent is running, module and version match source context, and the service account has the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role.
Check your understanding
Did the snapshot show the expected variables and stack frames? If not, re-check mapping and agent initialization.

screens.title: Cloud Run walkthrough: deploy, enable, set points
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough condenses the lab steps into a clear sequence you can follow. First, prepare the Flask application with the debugger library and requirements as shown. Add the enable call using K_SERVICE and K_REVISION for module and version. Next create the Dockerfile as provided and build your container. Deploy to Cloud Run using gcloud run deploy with a service name and region; note the service URL after deployment. In the Cloud Debugger console, select your project and the deployed service, open main dot P Y file, and set a snapshot on the intermediate calculation line inside the calculate route. Trigger that route with curl and then return to the Console to find the snapshot and inspect num, result, and intermediate_value. After that, set a logpoint on the response construction line with message DEBUG: Greeting for user: {user_input}, call the root URL, and verify that the injected log appears in Cloud Logging. Finally, delete your snapshot and logpoint to avoid lingering overhead. This sequence gives you practical familiarity with the full lifecycle from code to Console evidence. Cloud Run walkthrough: deploy, enable, set points means prepare code with the agent, deploy to cloud run, set a snapshot and a logpoint, trigger endpoints, inspect results, and clean up points.. screens.title: Snapshot vs Logpoint — choose the right tool
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a snapshot and a logpoint depends on the depth of information you need and the expected frequency of hits. Snapshots capture the full execution state, including locals, globals, and the call stack, making them ideal for deep investigations of a single event or rare bug. But snapshots are typically captured only for a few hits to limit overhead and are therefore best used when you can trigger representative traffic. Logpoints are lighter: they inject a formatted message that can include evaluated expressions and stream results to Cloud Logging across many hits. Use logpoints to observe value distributions, counts, or to gather context across many requests. A frequent misconception is that logpoints replace the need for snapshots; they do not capture call stack or full local scope. Another mistake is placing snapshots in hot code paths; choose logpoints for high-frequency lines. For example, use a snapshot to capture a complex state leading to an incorrect calculation once, then deploy logpoints to monitor the frequency of that incorrect value in subsequent traffic. Snapshot

screens.title: Safety considerations and operational best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When using Cloud Debugger in production, safety and minimal operational impact are top priorities. First, permissions: ensure the runtime’s service account has the Cloud Debugger Debuggee IAM role so the agent can register debuggees and send information. Second, source mapping: Cloud Debugger must match running code to source; provide the module and version labels and, where appropriate, integrate source context. A common failure mode is mismatched version labels, which prevents snapshot placement. Third, data security: snapshots can reveal local variables and therefore potentially sensitive data. Avoid capturing personally identifiable information or credentials in snapshots or logpoint expressions unless proper access controls and auditing are in place. Fourth, minimal impact: limit snapshots, avoid complex expressions in logpoints, and remove points when finished. Finally, version control and process: track where you set temporary points and delete them as part of your incident close-out. These practices keep debugging effective without introducing new risks to production stability or data privacy. Safety considerations and operational best practices means grant least privilege, map source correctly, avoid sensitive captures, limit overhead, and always remove temporary points after investigation.. screens.title: Common errors and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When Cloud Debugger doesn't behave as expected, three areas account for most failures: source mapping, permissions, and agent initialization. Source mapping failures occur when module or version labels passed to the agent do not match the source context in the Console. The debugger cannot place snapshot points if it cannot reliably map a running binary to the displayed source; verify the version string and that your repository source context is available. Permission issues arise when the runtime service account lacks the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role; the agent will be unable to register debuggees and snapshots will not be recorded. Agent initialization problems occur when the enable call is not executed early in the application lifecycle, or exceptions prevent the agent from registering; wrap initialization in a try/except and log a safe message on failure so your app still starts. A practical troubleshooting flow: check agent logs for initialization messages, confirm IAM roles, verify module/version labels, and then attempt a low-volume snapshot trigger to confirm mapping. These checks resolve the majority of setup problems quickly. Common errors and troubleshooting means if points fail, inspect agent logs, confirm cloud debugger debuggee role, and verify module/version mapping to your source context.. Troubleshooting › Common Errors
Source mapping error
Cause: module/version mismatch. Fix: update agent labels or provide source context so the Console can map lines to deployed code.
Permission failure
Cause: missing Cloud Debugger Debuggee role. Fix: grant the role to the runtime service account and retry registration.

  • Verify module/version matches the Console's source view.

fullNarratorScript:
When a bug only appears in production, stopping the service or redeploying to add debug logs is often impractical. Cloud Debugger gives you a different path: you can capture application state or inject temporary logs into a running instance without taking traffic offline. In this lesson you will see how snapshot points capture variables and call stacks when a specific line executes, and how logpoints let you write ephemeral log messages that appear in Cloud Logging. We’ll also cover how to enable the debugger agent, the importance of accurate module and version labels, and permission checks for safe operation. You will walk through a Cloud Run Python example where the debugger captures an intermediate value and then a logpoint injects a debug message. Finally, you’ll learn the core safety practices: limit snapshot hits, avoid capturing sensitive data, and remove temporary points after use. By the end you will understand why Cloud Debugger reduces mean time to resolution for elusive production bugs and when to prefer a snapshot versus a logpoint.

Over the next screens you will acquire four concrete skills that make production debugging safer and faster. First, you will be able to explain what Cloud Debugger does and why non-intrusive inspection matters. That helps you choose the right tool when stopping a service is unacceptable. Second, you will learn how to set snapshot points and logpoints, and when each is the better choice to gather runtime evidence. You will practice the mental model of snapshot equals frozen state and logpoint equals streaming observation. Third, you will integrate the debugger with common GCP environments and languages by adding the debugger agent and assigning correct module and version identifiers, ensuring the console can map running code to source. Finally, you will adopt safety and operational best practices: minimal snapshot hits, permission checks, avoiding sensitive data capture, and cleaning temporary points after use. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can self-check when you have reached practical readiness.

In this second objectives screen we focus on the practical outcomes you should achieve. You will be able to add the debugger agent to Python, Java, Node. js, Go, or PHP applications and set the module and version so Cloud Debugger can match running code to source. You will know how to use the GCP Console or the gcloud CLI to place snapshot points and logpoints, trigger them, and inspect captured values or logs. You will perform a Cloud Run walkthrough where you deploy a Flask app, set a snapshot to capture an intermediate calculation, and create a logpoint to log a greeting message. Finally, you will be able to reason about trade-offs: snapshots provide deep state but have higher overhead on first hits; logpoints are lightweight but only show expressions you choose to emit. This practical focus helps you choose the right technique for reducing mean time to resolution in real production incidents.

Cloud Debugger is a production-safe inspector that captures state from a running application without stopping it. Think of it as taking a photograph of program state when a particular line executes. That photograph shows local variables, globals, and the full call stack for that instant. The key advantage is that you do not interrupt live traffic. This matters because many bugs only appear under production data patterns, specific traffic levels, or timing conditions that are hard to reproduce locally. A common misconception is that non-intrusive means zero overhead — in practice the debugger minimizes impact but capturing snapshots or evaluating complex expressions can add small overhead for the first few hits. Use snapshots sparingly and prefer logpoints for repeated checks. For example, when a balance calculation occasionally returns the wrong value only under peak load, a snapshot on the calculation line reveals the exact operand values and call sequence that led to the error without forcing a restart. Remember: snapshot equals deep, momentary inspection; logpoint equals lightweight observation over time. Which will you choose when investigating an intermittent production error?

A snapshot point lifecycle has three clear stages: placement, capture, and inspection. First, place the snapshot at a precise line in the source where you want to freeze state. In the Console you click the line number and choose a snapshot; via tooling you may set the point programmatically. Second, when a request executes and hits that line, Cloud Debugger captures a snapshot that includes local variables, global variables, and the call stack. By default the system captures only the first few hits to keep overhead low. Third, the snapshot appears in the console where you can inspect values, step through the captured stack frames, and understand the flow that produced the bug. A common mistake is placing snapshots in hot loops or frequently-run lines; that can cause many captures and unnecessary overhead. For a concrete example, set a snapshot on the intermediate calculation in a customer billing route, trigger the route with representative input, and review captured variables to find where rounding or unexpected data entered the computation. Always remove snapshot points after you finish debugging. Logpoints let you inject temporary logging statements into running code so you can observe expressions over time without redeploying. Unlike snapshots, a logpoint emits a log message to Cloud Logging whenever its line is executed, and you can include expressions like user ID or action names inside the message. Use logpoints when you need repeated observations or want to monitor a value trend across requests. For instance, if you suspect a greeting service returns incorrect personalization occasionally, a logpoint that logs the resolved greeting input lets you see many instances across traffic and spot patterns. A frequent misconception is that logpoints can inspect full local state like snapshots; they can evaluate expressions but do not provide the full call-stack capture. Also avoid logging sensitive data by accident. Logpoints are ideal for low-overhead checks and for building time-based understanding of a problem before committing to a deeper snapshot capture. Cloud Debugger requires a debugger agent or library in your application so that running instances can communicate with the Cloud Debugger service. The agent is available in language-specific forms for Java, Python, Node. js, Go, and PHP. For managed environments like App Engine and Cloud Run, you typically initialize the agent early in application startup and include module and version identifiers; for GKE and Compute Engine you install the appropriate library into the container or VM. The agent authenticates using the service account attached to the runtime, which must have the Cloud Debugger Debuggee IAM role. A common pitfall is forgetting to supply accurate module or version labels. If those values do not match the source context visible in the Console, you will be unable to set points because the Console cannot map running code lines to your repository. For example, in a Python Flask app on GKE you add the googleclouddebugger enable call at boot and pass module='my-flask-app' and version='v1.0.0' so the debugger identifies the deployed source. Always initialize the agent as early as possible so the process can register before handling traffic.

Second, source mapping: Cloud Debugger must match running code to source; provide the module and version labels and, where appropriate, integrate source context. A common failure mode is mismatched version labels, which prevents snapshot placement. Third, data security: snapshots can reveal local variables and therefore potentially sensitive data. Avoid capturing personally identifiable information or credentials in snapshots or logpoint expressions unless proper access controls and auditing are in place. Fourth, minimal impact: limit snapshots, avoid complex expressions in logpoints, and remove points when finished. Finally, version control and process: track where you set temporary points and delete them as part of your incident close-out. These practices keep debugging effective without introducing new risks to production stability or data privacy. Safety considerations and operational best practices means grant least privilege, map source correctly, avoid sensitive captures, limit overhead, and always remove temporary points after investigation.. When Cloud Debugger doesn't behave as expected, three areas account for most failures: source mapping, permissions, and agent initialization. Source mapping failures occur when module or version labels passed to the agent do not match the source context in the Console. The debugger cannot place snapshot points if it cannot reliably map a running binary to the displayed source; verify the version string and that your repository source context is available. Permission issues arise when the runtime service account lacks the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role; the agent will be unable to register debuggees and snapshots will not be recorded. Agent initialization problems occur when the enable call is not executed early in the application lifecycle, or exceptions prevent the agent from registering; wrap initialization in a try/except and log a safe message on failure so your app still starts. A practical troubleshooting flow: check agent logs for initialization messages, confirm IAM roles, verify module/version labels, and then attempt a low-volume snapshot trigger to confirm mapping. These checks resolve the majority of setup problems quickly. Common errors and troubleshooting means if points fail, inspect agent logs, confirm cloud debugger debuggee role, and verify module/version mapping to your source context.. Let’s summarize three compact ideas to remember. First, Cloud Debugger enables non-intrusive inspection: it captures snapshots or injects logpoints into running services so you can observe state without stopping traffic. Second, snapshots and logpoints serve different purposes: use snapshots for deep, one-off captures of local variables and the call stack, and use logpoints for lightweight, repeated observations recorded to Cloud Logging. Third, setup and safety matter: initialize the debugger agent early with correct module and version identifiers, ensure the runtime service account has the Cloud Debugger Debuggee role, avoid capturing sensitive data, and remove points after use.
